questions.stem: Find the number of ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers with x·y = 3(x + y) + 10.

hint.level_0: Move all terms to one side and complete the rectangle (x − a)(y − a). What constant appears, and why are both factors forced positive?

solution_steps: 19 > 3² so both factors are positive; each ordered factorization gives one solution.
questions.solution: Step 1 — xy − 3x − 3y = 10 ⇒ $(x-3)$(y−3) = 3²+10 = 19. Step 2 — 19 > 3² so both factors are positive; each ordered factorization gives one solution. Step 3 — Answer = d(19) = 2.

questions.stem: For how many positive integers n is n² + 40 a perfect square?

hint.level_0: If n²+N = m², then (m−n)(m+n) = N. What constraints (positivity, parity) pin down the count?

solution_steps: Each valid factor pair gives one n=(e−d)/2.
questions.solution: Step 1 — m²−n²=40 ⇒ (m−n)(m+n)=40 with m−n<m+n, same parity. Step 2 — Each valid factor pair gives one n=(e−d)/2. Step 3 — Count = 2.

questions.stem: How many positive integers n ≤ 60 satisfy 2ⁿ ≡ 1 (mod 7)?

hint.level_0: The powers of 2 mod 7 cycle with some period (the order). For which n is the residue 1?

solution_steps: The order of 2 mod 7 is 3; 2ⁿ ≡ 1 iff 3 | n.
questions.solution: Step 1 — The order of 2 mod 7 is 3; 2ⁿ ≡ 1 iff 3 | n. Step 2 — Count multiples of 3 up to 60: ⌊60/3⌋. Step 3 — = 20.

questions.stem: For how many positive integers n ≤ 100 is (n² + 5) divisible by (n + 1)?

hint.level_0: Divide n²+c by n+d with remainder — the remainder is a constant. When does n+d divide that constant?

solution_steps: Count n with (n+1) a divisor of 6 in range.
questions.solution: Step 1 — n²+5 = (n+1)(n−1) + (1²+5); so (n+1) | (1²+5) = 6. Step 2 — Count n with (n+1) a divisor of 6 in range. Step 3 — = 3.
